system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2122-05-23 14:36:00 to 2122-05-25 17:15:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted for monitoring after undergoing his third transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) procedure for hepatocellular carcinoma. He tolerated the procedure well but developed expected post-embolization symptoms including right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and a significant transient elevation in liver enzymes. He also experienced temporary urinary retention requiring a straight catheterization, which resolved. His chronic conditions—alcoholic and hepatitis C-related cirrhosis, thrombocytopenia, and ulcerative colitis—were managed throughout the stay. Liver function tests peaked but began to improve, and symptoms were controlled with supportive care. He was discharged home in stable condition with updated medications and follow-up plans.
problems: Nonspecific elevation of levels of transaminase or lactic acid dehydrogenase [LDH]
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma

Brief Hospital Course:
BRIEF HOSPITAL COURSE
======================
Mr. ___ is a ___ year old gentleman with HCC s/p TACE, HCV, and 
EtOH cirrhosis with new onset subjective fevers/chills at home 
after TACE two weeks ago. He was afebrile throughout his hosital 
course. Chills were likely due to mild bronchitis (vs. post-TACE 
syndrome). Blood cultures, urine culture, and chest xray were 
all unremarkable. He was noted to have a new right upper 
extremity resting tremor with mild rigidity. This was felt to be 
a side effect from the metochlopramide and/or prochlorperizine 
he got after TACE. He had mild nausea (normal TSH, cortisol) and 
was tolerating a low sodium diet prior to discharge. He was 
discharged home w/ follow up in the transplant clinic and with 
his oncologist, as well as neurology. He was instructed to try 
lidocaine jelly, tramadol BID, and acetaminophen (<2g daily) for 
his pain, and to avoid compazine and reglan.

ACTIVE ISSUES
==============
# Subjective fever and chills: Given his history of HCC and 
cirrhosis, he is at increased risk for infection. He reported 
fevers and chills at home (though did not take his temperature), 
but there were no documented fevers in the ED or on the floor. 
Cultures were negative x24 hours, and infectious work-up was 
unrevealing (CXR showed atelectasis). Overall this seems most 
consistent w/ bronchitis given his mild non-productive cough and 
lack of opacities on CXR.  This could also be indicative of 
postembolization syndrome, which occurs in ~90% of patients 
following TACE, manifested by fever, malaise, right upper 
quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. He was never febrile, but 
did complain of chronic RUQ pain, nausea. 

# Extrapyramidal side effects of anti-emetics: He was noted to 
have cog-wheeling + resting tremor on exam by the accepting 
team. He reports that these symptoms began the day after his 
last hospitalization, during which he got large doses of  
metoclopramide and prochlorperazine. He reported initial 
dysarthria, which was not noted during this admission. We added 
both metoclopramide and prochlorperazine to his allergy list 
(ondansetron is less likely to cause EPS). He will follow up 
with neurology as an outpatient. Some studies have shown 
anti-cholinergics can treat EPS; as such, he was given oral 
diphenhydramine at night. In terms of his nausea, cortisol was 
normal. He tolerated a low sodium diet despite nausea (could be 
post-TACE picture, as above).
- QTc 438 on ___.
- Avoid metoclopramide and compazine.

# Hepatocellular CA s/p TACE: He is currently listed on the 
transplant list with ___ MELD exception points. Lab MELD was ~10. 
He had recurrent HCC at site of prior HCC, but was still within 
criteria. As such, he underwent TACE ___, which was 
complicated by N/V, abdominal pain, severe transaminitis (which 
was treated symptomatically).  For pain at the site of the 
procedure (no concerning findings on RUQ u/s), he was started on 
tramadol 50mg q12 hours, with lidocaine patch for flank.

CHRONIC ISSUES
===============
# Chronic hepatitis C and alcoholic cirhosis: Complicated by 
ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, SBP, and recurrent 
hepatocellular CA. He was continued on SBP prophylaxis. He was 
continued on home lactulose, rifaximin, 
furosemide/spironolactone, and nadolol.  

# Pancytopenia (Anemia/leukopenia/thrombocytopenia): Chronic, 
likely due to liver disease.  

# Hypertension: Continued home nadolol, spironolactone, and 
furosemide.  

# Ulcerative colitis: Continued home mesalamine.

Brief Hospital Course:
BRIEF HOSPITAL COURSE
======================
Mr. ___ is a ___ year old gentleman with HCC s/p TACE, HCV, and 
EtOH cirrhosis with new onset subjective fevers/chills at home 
after TACE two weeks ago. He was afebrile throughout his hosital 
course. Chills were likely due to mild bronchitis (vs. post-TACE 
syndrome). Blood cultures, urine culture, and chest xray were 
all unremarkable. He was noted to have a new right upper 
extremity resting tremor with mild rigidity. This was felt to be 
a side effect from the metochlopramide and/or prochlorperizine 
he got after TACE. He had mild nausea (normal TSH, cortisol) and 
was tolerating a low sodium diet prior to discharge. He was 
discharged home w/ follow up in the transplant clinic and with 
his oncologist, as well as neurology. He was instructed to try 
lidocaine jelly, tramadol BID, and acetaminophen (<2g daily) for 
his pain, and to avoid compazine and reglan.

ACTIVE ISSUES
==============
# Subjective fever and chills: Given his history of HCC and 
cirrhosis, he is at increased risk for infection. He reported 
fevers and chills at home (though did not take his temperature), 
but there were no documented fevers in the ED or on the floor. 
Cultures were negative x24 hours, and infectious work-up was 
unrevealing (CXR showed atelectasis). Overall this seems most 
consistent w/ bronchitis given his mild non-productive cough and 
lack of opacities on CXR.  This could also be indicative of 
postembolization syndrome, which occurs in ~90% of patients 
following TACE, manifested by fever, malaise, right upper 
quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. He was never febrile, but 
did complain of chronic RUQ pain, nausea. 

# Extrapyramidal side effects of anti-emetics: He was noted to 
have cog-wheeling + resting tremor on exam by the accepting 
team. He reports that these symptoms began the day after his 
last hospitalization, during which he got large doses of  
metoclopramide and prochlorperazine. He reported initial 
dysarthria, which was not noted during this admission. We added 
both metoclopramide and prochlorperazine to his allergy list 
(ondansetron is less likely to cause EPS). He will follow up 
with neurology as an outpatient. Some studies have shown 
anti-cholinergics can treat EPS; as such, he was given oral 
diphenhydramine at night. In terms of his nausea, cortisol was 
normal. He tolerated a low sodium diet despite nausea (could be 
post-TACE picture, as above).

# Hepatocellular CA s/p TACE: He is currently listed on the 
transplant list with ___ MELD exception points. Lab MELD was ~10. 
He had recurrent HCC at site of prior HCC, but was still within 
criteria. As such, he underwent TACE ___, which was 
complicated by N/V, abdominal pain, severe transaminitis (which 
was treated symptomatically).  For pain at the site of the 
procedure (no concerning findings on RUQ u/s), he was started on 
tramadol 50mg q12 hours, with lidocaine patch for flank.

CHRONIC ISSUES
===============
# Chronic hepatitis C and alcoholic cirhosis: Complicated by

hepatocellular CA. He was continued on SBP prophylaxis. He was 
continued on home lactulose, rifaximin,

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in last night with chills and feeling feverish. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I was at home and suddenly started shaking—real bad chills. I didn’t have a thermometer, but I felt hot, like I had a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any cough or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little cough, no phlegm. Started the same night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any pain anywhere?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My right side, near the old TACE site. It’s sharp, but I’ve had it before. Started around the same time as the chills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And how about nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit of nausea, but not bad. I’ve been using the meds you gave me after the last procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Which ones are you taking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Prochlorperazine for nausea, and hydromorphone for pain. I flushed the old morphine—didn’t like how it made me feel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned trouble speaking and handwriting before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, right after the last hospital stay. My speech was slurred, and my right hand shook. It’s better now, but the tremor’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed a slight tremor and some stiffness in your right hand today. That could be from the anti-nausea meds—prochlorperazine and metoclopramide can sometimes cause that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, really? I thought it was from the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not the pain meds. These anti-nausea drugs can affect movement in some people. We’re going to stop those and add something safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I shouldn’t take them again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, we’ll avoid them from now on. We’ll update your allergies so no one prescribes them by mistake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve ordered blood tests and a chest X-ray to check for infection. Your white blood cell count was low, which can happen with cirrhosis, but we want to be sure there’s no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had low counts before. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s chronic for you, related to your liver disease. But it does mean you’re more vulnerable to infections, so we’re being cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows low lung volume and some mild atelectasis—basically, your lungs aren’t fully inflated. No pneumonia, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the cough isn’t serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely mild bronchitis—viral inflammation of the airways. It should resolve on its own. The chills might be from that, or from post-TACE syndrome, which can cause flu-like symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. But I wasn’t actually running a fever here, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’ve been afebrile—no fever recorded. So it was likely a subjective fever, which still feels real to you, but not picked up on the thermometer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did an ultrasound to check for fluid in your abdomen. Good news—it shows no ascites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Given your cirrhosis, we watch for that. Your liver enzymes are elevated, but they’ve improved since admission—likely from the recent TACE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain and labs are just from the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. The bronchitis explains the chills and cough. The tremor is from the anti-nausea meds. We’ve started diphenhydramine at night—it may help with the tremor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Won’t that make me sleepy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might, but it’s only at night. And it’s important not to take it with tramadol—could increase drowsiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable, and all cultures came back negative—no infection. We’re comfortable discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the tremor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve set up a neurology follow-up. The diphenhydramine should help. Most importantly, avoid prochlorperazine and metoclopramide in the future.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding a lidocaine patch for the flank pain—apply it twice daily. Keep using tramadol as needed, but no more than 2 grams of acetaminophen a day to protect your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Continue all your regular meds for cirrhosis, blood pressure, and colitis. And keep your transplant and oncology follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted for evaluation of subjective fevers and chills two weeks after his recent transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) for hepatocellular carcinoma. He remained afebrile during the hospitalization, and infectious workup—including blood and urine cultures and chest imaging—was negative, with findings most consistent with viral bronchitis. His right upper quadrant pain was attributed to post-TACE syndrome. A new resting tremor and cogwheeling in the right hand were identified and determined to be extrapyramidal side effects from prior use of prochlorperazine and metoclopramide, both of which were discontinued and added to his allergy list. He was started on diphenhydramine for tremor management and a lidocaine patch for localized pain. His chronic conditions, including alcoholic and hepatitis C-related cirrhosis, hypertension, and ulcerative colitis, were maintained on existing regimens. He was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up arranged in neurology, oncology, and transplant clinics.
